introduction-mlops-on-steroids.core: LLM operations amplify MLOps challenges. Models with billions of parameters need massive GPU memory, generation is sequential and memory-hungry (the KV cache), costs scale with tokens, and customisation calls for efficient techniques like LoRA.

first_principles.problem: Teams try to serve a 70B model like a small classifier and run out of GPU memory and budget.
truths: Tokens are the unit of cost.

analogy.title: Moving from a car to a cargo ship
analogy.story: The same principles of navigation apply, but at a scale that changes every logistics decision.
analogy.breaks: Hosted APIs avoid much of this, at the cost of control and per-token pricing.

check.q: Why is serving LLMs harder than serving small ML models?
check.a: Their enormous memory requirements, sequential generation with large KV caches, and per-token cost scaling.

the-vram-bottleneck-and-quantization.core: Model memory ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter: 70B parameters at FP16 (2 bytes) is about 140 GB. Quantisation stores weights in fewer bits (INT8 or INT4 using methods like GPTQ, AWQ or GGUF), shrinking memory 2–4x with modest quality loss.

first_principles.problem: A 70B model doesn't fit on available GPUs, and buying more is expensive or impossible.
derivation: Memory ≈ params × bytes + KV cache + overhead.

analogy.title: Compressing photos from RAW to JPEG
analogy.story: Much smaller files that look almost the same for most uses.
analogy.breaks: Aggressive quantisation (below 4-bit) can degrade reasoning noticeably.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A single 48–80 GB GPU becomes feasible.

check.q: Roughly how much GPU memory do the weights of a 7B-parameter model need at FP16?
check.a: About 14 GB (7 billion × 2 bytes), plus KV cache and overhead.

efficient-serving-the-magic-of-vllm.core: Generating each token needs the attention keys and values of all previous tokens (the KV cache), which can be huge and fragmented. vLLM's PagedAttention manages KV memory in pages like an OS's virtual memory, and continuous batching adds requests mid-flight, which multiplies throughput.

first_principles.problem: Naive serving wastes 60–80% of KV-cache memory to fragmentation and handles few concurrent requests.
truths: KV cache grows with sequence length × batch.
derivation: **Continuous batching**: add and remove requests per step.

analogy.title: A restaurant that seats diners as soon as a seat frees
analogy.story: Instead of waiting for a whole table to finish before seating the next group, any free seat is filled immediately.
analogy.breaks: Very long contexts still exhaust KV memory, so you need limits and offloading.

example.title: Serving with vLLM
example.outcome: LLM serving that uses GPU memory efficiently.

check.a: KV-cache memory fragmentation and waste, by allocating KV memory in on-demand blocks like virtual-memory pages.

token-economics-the-currency-of-ai.core: LLMs process tokens (roughly ¾ of a word), and cost, latency and limits are all denominated in tokens. Output tokens usually cost more than input tokens. Cost per request ≈ input × input price + output × output price, which drives design choices.

first_principles.problem: A chatbot sends the whole conversation history plus long system prompts with every request, and the bill explodes.
truths: Every token in and out costs money.
Output generation is slower and pricier.
derivation: **Route** easy queries to smaller, cheaper models.

analogy.title: A taxi meter
analogy.story: You pay for every kilometre, so the shortest route and the right-sized car save money.
analogy.breaks: Over-trimming context hurts answer quality, so balance cost against accuracy.

example.title: Cost per request

steps.label: Lever
steps.detail: Halving the prompt saves about $4.5k per million requests.

code.text:
inp, out = 3000, 500
cost = inp/1e6 * 3.00 + out/1e6 * 15.00   # $ per 1M tokens
print(f"${cost:.4f} per request")       # ≈ $0.0165; ×1M requests ≈ $16.5k

example.outcome: LLM features designed with costs in mind.

check.q: Why do output tokens typically cost more than input tokens?
check.a: They're generated sequentially, one at a time, which takes more compute time per token than processing input in parallel.

context-window-optimization.core: The context window caps total tokens (input + output). Longer contexts cost more, slow responses and can dilute attention ('lost in the middle'). Optimise by retrieving only relevant chunks, summarising history, ordering key information well and caching stable prefixes.

first_principles.problem: Stuffing 100k tokens of documents into every prompt is slow and expensive, and answers get worse.
truths: Cost and latency grow with context length.
Models attend unevenly across long contexts.
Much context is irrelevant to the question.
derivation: **Retrieve** top-k relevant chunks (RAG) rather than dumping everything.
**Place** critical instructions at the start or end.

analogy.title: Packing a suitcase for a trip
analogy.story: Take only what you'll need; an overstuffed case is heavy and you can't find anything.
analogy.breaks: Some tasks genuinely need long context (whole-codebase analysis), so use long-context models deliberately.

check.q: What is the 'lost in the middle' problem?
check.a: Models tend to use information at the start and end of long contexts better than information buried in the middle.

customization-the-problem-with-fine-tuni.core: Base models may lack your domain style, format or knowledge. Full fine-tuning updates every weight, which needs huge GPU memory (weights, gradients and optimizer states, often 3–4x the model size) and produces a full model copy per variant.

first_principles.problem: Fine-tuning a 70B model needs a cluster of GPUs and produces a 140 GB copy for every customer variant.
truths: Training memory far exceeds inference memory.
Storing many full copies is wasteful.
derivation: Fine-tune for **style, format or narrow tasks** only.

analogy.title: Rewriting an entire textbook to add a chapter
analogy.story: Reprinting thousands of pages for a small addition is wasteful.
analogy.breaks: Fine-tuning doesn't reliably add facts; use RAG for knowledge.

example.title: Memory for full fine-tuning

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Even a 7B model needs serious hardware.

example.outcome: you understand why full fine-tuning is expensive.

check.q: Why does full fine-tuning need much more memory than inference?
check.a: Training stores gradients and optimizer states for every parameter in addition to the weights.

adapters-lora-and-qlora.core: LoRA freezes the base model and trains small low-rank adapter matrices (often under 1% of parameters) added to attention layers. QLoRA also quantises the frozen base to 4-bit, letting you fine-tune large models on a single GPU. Adapters are small files you can swap per task or tenant.

first_principles.problem: You need many customised model variants without the cost of full fine-tuning and full copies.
truths: Weight updates during fine-tuning are often low-rank.
derivation: **Add** low-rank matrices A·B (rank r = 8–64) to target layers.
**Serve** a shared base + per-task adapters (multi-LoRA serving).

analogy.title: Sticky notes in a textbook
analogy.story: Instead of rewriting the book, you add notes on key pages, and different students can have different notes.
analogy.breaks: Adapters have limited capacity, and some deep behaviour changes need full fine-tuning.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A tailored model in hours on one GPU, as a 50 MB adapter.

code.text:
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
cfg = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"], lora_dropout=0.05)
model = get_peft_model(base_model, cfg)
model.print_trainable_parameters()  # ~0.2% trainable

check.q: What does QLoRA add on top of LoRA?
check.a: It quantises the frozen base model to 4-bit, drastically reducing memory so large models can be fine-tuned on a single GPU.
